extracted.intended_audience: readers of Renaissance moral/philosophical essays; general educated readers and literary scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and extraction of evaluative maxims, social observations, and practical recommendations found in Montaigne's Essays (selected chapters). The chunk contains reflections on courage, customs, divine providence, civic ideas, and habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: True victory
rubrics_metrics.description: Victoria nulla est, Quam quae confessor animo quoque subjugat hostes. (No victory is complete, which the conquered do not admit to be so.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that forcing terror to extort a submissive word or confession is the essence of some peoples' idea of victory (example: Hungarians reduce enemies to their discretion then often release them). He contrasts physical advantages (arms, armour, fortune, fencing skill) as borrowed or accidental with true moral victory, which resides in the conquered's inner admission. Examples and anti-patterns: using threats to obtain mere submission is a hollow triumph; the honour of valour lies in constancy of heart, not in material superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valour as stability of courage
rubrics_metrics.description: Valour is stability, not of legs and arms, but of the courage and the soul; it does not lie in the goodness of our horse or our arms but in our own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate bravery by constancy of spirit rather than external means. Montaigne gives instances (falls obstinate in courage, 'If his legs fail him, he fights on his knees') and contrasts death without surrender to being truly unconquered. Example figures: Leonidas and his men at Thermopylae, Captain Iscolas, whose deliberate stand to make the enemy pay dearly is presented as a higher glory than many combined victories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triumphant defeats
rubrics_metrics.description: There are defeats more triumphant than victories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne claims certain defeats (e.g., Leonidas at Thermopylae; Captain Iscolas' sacrifice) have greater moral glory than ostensible victories. The criterion for greatness is the nature of the resistance and the honour shown in the encounter, not the outcome. Use of historical examples emphasizes that moral evaluation can invert apparent success/failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marital virtue as public testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: In some peoples, having several wives increases a man's reputation for valour; wives promote their husbands' desires and procure many spouses as testimony of his virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne presents this as a custom that, though jarring to many readers, is not 'monstrous' but rather a valid matrimonial virtue in that society. He supports cross-cultural acceptance by citing biblical and classical precedents (Sarah with Leah and Rachel's handmaids; Livia; Stratonice). The guidance is to suspend immediate moral condemnation and recognize different social logics behind practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspending judgment across customs
rubrics_metrics.description: I am not guilty of the common error of judging another by myself. I easily believe that in another’s humour which is contrary to my own; and though I find myself engaged to one certain form, I do not oblige others to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne endorses openness to diverse manners of life, languages, songs, and customs (e.g., he finds a foreign love-song 'perfectly Anacreontic'). Practical advice: avoid imposing one's own standards as universal; evaluate foreign practices on their own terms and look for internal coherence or merit rather than reflexive condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sober judgment of divine ordinances
rubrics_metrics.description: We should not seek to affirm and support our religion by the prosperity of our enterprises; nothing is so firmly believed as what we least know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use worldly success or failure as proof of divine favour or disapproval — doing so risks making faith contingent on fortune and can lead the vulgar to lose belief when events go ill. Montaigne gives historical examples (Rochelabeille, Moncontour, Jarnac, Lepanto) and cautions against reading providence through the narrow lens of events. He quotes scripture and Church fathers to argue for humility before divine mysteries and warns against attempting to 'reduce divine things to our balance.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding pleasures even at the expense of life (moderated)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is high time to die when there is more ill than good in living; to preserve life to our own torment is contrary to nature; yet one must be cautious about using death as an instrument to renounce honours and goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes ancient opinions (Stoics, Epicureans) that recommend death over a miserable life and recounts Seneca's counsel to Lucilius and St. Hilary's extreme ascetic prayers for his daughter's death. The guidance: accept that self-removal can be reasonable in certain circumstances, but avoid unreflective or prescriptive exhortations that use death to enforce philosophical or religious ideals without moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortune often acts by the rule of reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The inconstancy and various motions of Fortune may reasonably make us expect she should present us with all sorts of faces; sometimes Fortune's effects resemble intentional, artful or providential acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne collects many anecdotes (poisoned wine killing the Pope and sparing the son; Protogenes' sponge producing an accidental flourish; Jason of Pheres cured by a battle wound; Isabel of England thrown into a safer harbour) to argue that fortune can appear to have design and may surpass human prudence. Practical implication: expect unpredictability, see purpose where chance may operate, and avoid simplistic readings of events as purely random or purely moral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public exchange for matching needs (civic reform)
rubrics_metrics.description: There might be in every city a certain place to which such as stood in need of anything might repair, and have their business entered by an officer appointed for that purpose (buyers, sellers, servants, masters, artificers, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a concrete administrative recommendation to improve public correspondence and to prevent talented but needy people from dying in obscurity. Montaigne cites examples of learned men who died poor and argues such a system would facilitate mutual assistance and employment — a practical civic improvement rather than mere speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household journal keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a journal in which to set down all the remarkable occurrences and daily memorials of the history of a house: visitors, travels, marriages, deaths, reception of news, change of principal servants, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne's father required a steward to maintain a household journal (distinct from small cash accounts). Benefits include helping memory, resolving doubts about dates or events, and preserving institutional memory. Montaigne recommends reviving this ancient custom for personal and administrative usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clothing as custom rather than natural necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: The fashion of wearing clothes is largely custom; many peoples live with very little clothing even in cold climates, and nature may have originally provided sufficient covering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne challenges assumptions about necessity of specific garments, adducing examples (nation of Indians and Moors, Egyptians vs Persians, Massinissa, Caesar, Poles' king Stephen Bathory) and citing Plato's health advice to give head and feet little covering. Practical takeaway: evaluate clothing norms as cultural conventions; consider health and habit rather than blind imitation of fashion.
